blocks.text: Some passages on the honey-making of bees which the Greek Fathers cite as if from Scripture.

Bees are commended above all for their skill in making honey. On this, in the sacred text of the Hebrews, [col. 511] you will find only Iud. XIV, 8: And behold, a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey! A swarm of bees, and honey: that is, a swarm of honey-making bees, or of bees producing honey, by the figure ἓν διὰ δυοῖν [hen dia dyoin]. But the Greek Fathers bring out three other texts from their own store. The first is Psalmi CXVII, (Hebraeis CXVIII,) 12: Ἐκύκλωσάν με, ὡσεὶ μέλισσαι κηρίον· [Ekyklōsan me, hōsei melissai kērion] They surrounded me, as bees a honeycomb. So Augustine, Jerome and Theodoret cite it from the Greek version. Nor do our editions have anything else. The Ethiopic also follows the same. And the Arabic, which I have in manuscript, reads احتاطوا بي مثل النحل بالشهد [iḥtāṭū bī mithl al-naḥl bi-l-shahd] They surrounded me, as bees a honeycomb. But for الشهد [al-shahd], that is, honeycomb, the printed editions have الشمع [al-shamʿ] wax, as if the Arabs had read κηρὸν [kēron] in the Greek, not κηρίον [kērion]. In the Hebrew, however, one reads only סבוני כדבורים, They surrounded me, like bees. And that κηρίον [kērion] seems to have been wrongly added. For David is speaking of his enemies; and he does not compare them with bees that surround a honeycomb, since there is nothing hostile in that, but with bees that surround a man or a beast in a body, to sting with hostile stings. So in Statius, Thebaid book 10:

So, when a shepherd, about to plunder them, has driven the armed bees from their pumice cave, the fierce cloud roars, and they urge one another on with buzzing, and all fly into the face of the foe. — — —
But these matters have already been dealt with above.

[III, 366] The second text is Prov. VI, 8, where, after the much-celebrated (πολυθρύλλητον [polythryllēton]) passage on the ant, Go to the ant, O sluggard, etc., the Greek edition reads: Ἢ πορεύθητι πρὸς τὴν μέλισσαν, καὶ μάθε, ὡς ἐργάτις ἐστι, τήν τε ἐργασίαν ὡς σεμνὴν ποιεῖται· ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται. ποθεινὴ δέ ἐστι πᾶσι, καὶ ἐπίδοξος· καίπερ οὖσα τῇ ῥώμῃ ἀσθενὴς, τὴν σοφίαν τιμήσασα προήχθη. [Ē poreuthēti pros tēn melissan, kai mathe, hōs ergatis esti, tēn te ergasian hōs semnēn poieitai; hēs tous ponous basileis kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai. potheinē de esti pasi, kai epidoxos; kaiper ousa tē rhōmē asthenēs, tēn sophian timēsasa proēchthē.] Castalio rendered this in his version as follows: Or go to the bee, and learn how industrious she is, and how majestic a work she carries on: by whose labours both kings and private persons are wholesomely fed. And she is beloved and renowned among all; and, although weak in strength, she has nevertheless advanced by her zeal for wisdom. The Arabic version also: او انهب الي النحلة واعرف انها مثل الفاعل هي تعمل صناعتها طرفة عجيبة * واتعابها تحمل الي الملوك * والعامة يستعملوها لحفظ الصحة * وهي عند جميع الناس ماثورة مشرفة * مع ضعيفة في قوتها قدمت لانها اكرمت بالحكمة وفضلت * [aw inhab ilá al-naḥla wa-iʿrif annahā mithl al-fāʿil hiya taʿmal ṣināʿatahā ṭurfa ʿajība * wa-atʿābuhā tuḥmal ilá al-mulūk * wa-al-ʿāmma yastaʿmilūhā li-ḥifẓ al-ṣiḥḥa * wa-hiya ʿinda jamīʿ al-nās maʾthūra musharrafa * maʿa ḍaʿīfa fī quwwatihā qaddamat li-annahā ukrimat bi-l-ḥikma wa-fuḍḍilat *] Or go to the bee, and know that, like a workman, she fashions her work with wonderful art. And her labours are carried to kings, and the common people use them to preserve health. And she is excellent and noble among all men. Although she is weak in strength, she nevertheless excels, because she is commended for wisdom, [col. 512] and is outstanding. Many ancient writers cite the same passage: thus Clement of Alexandria, book 1 of the Stromata; Origen on Numbers, Homily 27, and on Isaiah, Homily 2; Basil on the Hexaemeron, Homily 8; Ambrose on the Hexaemeron, book 5, ch. 21; Jerome on Ezekiel, ch. 3; Theodoret, On Providence, Oration 5; Antiochus, Abbot of Saba, Homily 36; John of Damascus, book 2 of the Parallels, ch. 89. Yet, as Jerome rightly observes in the place cited, the Hebrew copies do not have this. Accordingly there is no trace of this passage in the Chaldee, the Syriac or the Vulgate version. And I have often wondered where the Greek translators took it from, as also certain other things which they insert here and there in various places. For it is not credible that they would have added these things of their own accord, unless they had found them already inserted in some copies of the Hebrews.
